--- title: "Uncertainty and stability" description: "A cross-validated score comes from one survey, and would move if other sites had been sampled. Drawing the sites again puts an interval on each model's score, and a paired comparison on the same draws says how sure a ranking of two models is." order: 5 categories: [validation, uncertainty] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A score from one survey is an estimate Most pages so far have reported a model's score as a single number. That number comes from one survey: had other sites on the same coast been sampled, the cross-validated RMSE would have come out higher or lower, and two models might have swapped places. Before a score is reported, or used to choose between models, it is worth knowing how far it could move. This page puts an interval on a cross-validated score, and shows that comparing two models needs an interval of its own, much narrower than either model's. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Resampling the sites gives a score its interval [Dependent data](../06-assumptions-limitations/dependent-data.qmd#resampling-whole-groups-measures-the-effective-sample-size) drew bootstrap samples of whole sites to see how far an estimate moves from one sample to the next. A score can be treated the same way. Cross-validation has already given every station an out-of-fold prediction, as on [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd#out-of-fold-predictions-are-pooled-into-one-score). A bootstrap sample draws the sites again, with replacement, keeps each drawn site's stations with their predictions, and works out the RMSE on them. Repeated a thousand times, this gives a thousand RMSEs. The middle 95% of them, from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile, is a 95% [confidence interval](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) for the score. Nothing is refitted, so a thousand samples take a second or two. The interval shows how much the score depends on which sites were scored. ## Two models are compared in pairs Two models scored on the same sites share most of what makes a score high or low. A site with a few very large catches raises every model's RMSE, and a site of near-empty stations lowers them all. So when the sites are drawn again, the two scores rise and fall together, and their intervals can overlap widely even when one model is better in almost every sample. A **paired comparison** works out the difference between the two scores within each bootstrap sample, so that what they share cancels. The interval of that difference says how sure the ranking is. ::: {.diagram} ![Two models scored on five resamples. Scored alone, each model's error moves widely from one resample to the next, and the two intervals overlap almost entirely. In pairs, the difference between the two errors is nearly the same in every resample, and its interval is short and clear of zero.](img/paired-comparison.svg){fig-alt="Two cards. Left, scored alone, the intervals overlap: five resamples, each with the error of model A, a blue dot, and of model B, an orange dot, joined by a short line. From one resample to the next both errors move together, between 3.4 and 5.3, and B is always a little lower. Below, model A's interval runs from 3.6 to 5.3 and model B's from 3.4 to 5.0, so the two overlap almost entirely. Right, in pairs, the difference is clear: the same five resamples give one green dot each, the error of B minus the error of A, between minus 0.4 and minus 0.2, all to the left of a dashed line at zero. Its interval is short and clear of zero. A note says a hard resample is hard for both models, so their errors rise and fall together; their difference cancels what they share, so it is far more certain than either error."} ::: Pairing needs both models to have predicted the same stations from the same folds, which is why every page in this section fits all its models on one set of folds. ## Worked example The models are three of the four on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd): - **Predicting the average**, with no skill. - **Linear regression**, the simple baseline. - **Random forest**. They are cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites as on that page, so their out-of-fold predictions and RMSEs are the same. A thousand bootstrap samples of the sites then give each score its interval, and give each pair of models a paired difference. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") with_inputs <- function(model) { recipe(reformulate(inputs, "abundance"), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> workflow(model) } forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression") models <- list( "Predicting the average" = with_inputs(null_model(mode = "regression")), "Linear regression" = with_inputs(linear_reg()), "Random forest" = with_inputs(forest) ) # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) { fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) }) scored <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |> mutate(site_id = survey$site_id, caught = survey$abundance) rmse_by_model <- function(data) { map_dbl(set_names(names(models)), \(m) rmse_vec(data$caught, data[[m]])) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| |--------:|-----:| | 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() caught = survey["abundance"].to_numpy() folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical] def with_inputs(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1) models = { "Predicting the average": DummyRegressor(), "Linear regression": LinearRegression(), "Random forest": forest, } # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"]) for name, model in models.items()} def rmse_by_model(rows): return {name: root_mean_squared_error(caught[rows], predicted[rows]) for name, predicted in out_of_fold.items()} pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [survey["site_id"].nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | |-----------:|--------:| | 800 | 160 | ::: ::: ::: The survey's 800 stations come from 160 sites, so each bootstrap sample draws 160 sites with replacement, some of them twice or more and others not at all. ### Each model's interval is wider than the gaps between the models ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(62) site_samples <- group_bootstraps(scored, group = site_id, times = 1000) # one row per bootstrap sample, one column per model scores <- map(site_samples$splits, \(s) as_tibble_row(rmse_by_model(analysis(s)))) |> list_rbind() intervals <- tibble( model = names(models), RMSE = rmse_by_model(scored), lower = map_dbl(scores, \(x) quantile(x, 0.025)), upper = map_dbl(scores, \(x) quantile(x, 0.975)) ) |> mutate(width = upper - lower) intervals |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | RMSE| lower| upper| width| |:----------------------|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |Predicting the average | 4.777| 4.071| 5.596| 1.525| |Linear regression | 4.388| 3.868| 4.971| 1.103| |Random forest | 4.321| 3.750| 4.945| 1.195|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} sites = survey["site_id"].to_numpy() site_rows = [np.flatnonzero(sites == s) for s in np.unique(sites)] # draw the sites again, with replacement, and score every model on their stations rng = np.random.default_rng(62) samples = [] for sample in range(1000): drawn = rng.integers(len(site_rows), size=len(site_rows)) rows = np.concatenate([site_rows[i] for i in drawn]) samples.append(rmse_by_model(rows)) scores = pd.DataFrame(samples) intervals = pd.DataFrame({ "model": list(models), "RMSE": list(rmse_by_model(np.arange(len(survey))).values()), "lower": scores.quantile(0.025).to_numpy(), "upper": scores.quantile(0.975).to_numpy(), }) intervals["width"] = intervals["upper"] - intervals["lower"] intervals.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | RMSE | lower | upper | width | |:-----------------------|-------:|--------:|--------:|--------:| | Predicting the average | 4.778 | 4.06 | 5.551 | 1.491 | | Linear regression | 4.389 | 3.851 | 4.947 | 1.095 | | Random forest | 4.249 | 3.691 | 4.841 | 1.15 | ::: ::: ::: Each RMSE is shown with its 95% interval: predicting the average 4.78 (4.07 to 5.60), linear regression 4.39 (3.87 to 4.97) and the random forest 4.32 (3.75 to 4.94). The intervals are 1.10 to 1.53 wide, more than twice the forest's lead of 0.46 over predicting the average, and many times its lead of 0.07 over linear regression. Read alone, the three intervals overlap, and cannot say which model is better: not even whether either model beats predicting the average. ### Pairing separates the forest from the average but not from linear regression ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} full <- rmse_by_model(scored) differences <- map(c("Predicting the average", "Linear regression"), \(other) { in_each_sample <- scores$`Random forest` - scores[[other]] tibble(`forest minus` = other, difference = full[["Random forest"]] - full[[other]], lower = quantile(in_each_sample, 0.025), upper = quantile(in_each_sample, 0.975), `samples with the forest lower` = mean(in_each_sample < 0)) }) |> list_rbind() differences |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|forest minus | difference| lower| upper| samples with the forest lower| |:----------------------|----------:|------:|------:|-----------------------------:| |Predicting the average | -0.456| -0.828| -0.071| 0.988| |Linear regression | -0.067| -0.218| 0.098| 0.802|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} full = rmse_by_model(np.arange(len(survey))) table_rows = [] for other in ["Predicting the average", "Linear regression"]: in_each_sample = scores["Random forest"] - scores[other] table_rows.append({"forest minus": other, "difference": full["Random forest"] - full[other], "lower": in_each_sample.quantile(0.025), "upper": in_each_sample.quantile(0.975), "samples with the forest lower": (in_each_sample < 0).mean()}) differences = pd.DataFrame(table_rows) differences.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | forest minus | difference | lower | upper | samples with the forest lower | |:-----------------------|-------------:|--------:|--------:|--------------------------------:| | Predicting the average | -0.529 | -0.776 | -0.268 | 1 | | Linear regression | -0.14 | -0.238 | -0.047 | 0.999 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paired_scores <- scores |> pivot_longer(c(`Predicting the average`, `Linear regression`), names_to = "other", values_to = "other_rmse") |> mutate(other = str_to_lower(other), other = fct_inorder(paste("Against", other)), better = if_else(`Random forest` < other_rmse, "Forest lower", "Forest higher")) limits <- range(c(scores$`Random forest`, paired_scores$other_rmse)) ggplot(paired_scores, aes(other_rmse, `Random forest`, colour = better)) + geom_abline(colour = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~other) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Forest lower" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Forest higher" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]), breaks = c("Forest lower", "Forest higher")) + coord_equal(xlim = limits, ylim = limits) + labs(x = "RMSE of the other model (individuals)", y = "RMSE of the forest (individuals)", colour = NULL) + guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The forest's RMSE against another model's in each of the 1,000 bootstrap samples of sites. Points below the dashed diagonal are samples in which the forest scored better. Against predicting the average, it did in 99% of samples. Against linear regression the points hug the diagonal, as the two scores rise and fall together, and the forest did better in 80%.](uncertainty-and-stability_files/figure-html/fig-pairs-1.png){#fig-pairs fig-alt='Two square scatter plots side by side, each with a dashed diagonal line. Each has 1,000 points, one per bootstrap sample, with the forest\'s RMSE on the vertical axis. In the left panel the horizontal axis is the RMSE of predicting the average; the points form a long cloud running from about 3.63 to 6.19 along it, almost all of them below the diagonal. In the right panel the horizontal axis is the RMSE of linear regression; the points form a long, narrow band lying along the diagonal, most of them just below it and some just above.' width=1600} ::: ::: ::: Against predicting the average, the forest's RMSE is lower by 0.46, with a paired 95% interval from −0.83 to −0.07. The interval lies clear of zero, and the forest scored better in 99% of the samples, although the two models' own intervals overlap. Against linear regression the paired interval runs from −0.22 to 0.10. At 0.32 wide, against 1.10 for the narrowest of the models' own intervals, it is far sharper, because the two scores move almost in step (their correlation across the samples is 0.97). It still covers zero. The forest did better in 80% of the samples, so the order on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) is not stable: on this survey, RMSE cannot tell the forest from linear regression. ## Overlapping intervals do not show that two models are alike Report each score with its interval and the number of sites behind it. Compare two models by their paired difference, never by whether their own intervals overlap: here every interval overlapped the others, and the forest still beat predicting the average in nearly every sample. A lead that holds in 80% of samples is not yet a result. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A cross-validated score comes from one survey, and would move if other sites had been sampled. A bootstrap of the sites over the out-of-fold predictions gives it an interval; here each model's 95% interval was 1.10 to 1.53 wide. - Two models are compared by a **paired comparison**: the difference in score within each bootstrap sample, on the same folds. What the two share cancels, so the paired interval is much narrower than either model's own. - The forest beat predicting the average in 99% of samples, although their own intervals overlapped. It beat linear regression in only 80%, and the paired interval covered zero. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Score the models with the MAE (`mae_vec()`) instead of the RMSE. Can the forest and linear regression be told apart now? 2. Draw single stations instead of whole sites (`bootstraps()` in place of `group_bootstraps()`). How much narrower do the intervals become, and why are they too narrow?
